content: Patients with a history of colitis should exercise caution when using antacids containing magnesium or aluminum, as these can interfere with the absorption of cefdinir. If antacids are necessary during cefdinir therapy, they should be taken at least two hours before or after the antibiotic. Similarly, iron supplements, including multivitamins containing iron, can also reduce cefdinir absorption. If iron supplementation is required, it should be administered at least two hours apart from cefdinir. Cefdinir is classified as a pregnancy category B medication, meaning that controlled studies in pregnant women have not shown evidence of fetal risk. However, it is unknown whether cefdinir is excreted in breast milk. The drug is minimally metabolized, has a half-life of approximately 100 minutes, and is primarily excreted in the urine, with 7-25% eliminated as unchanged drug. Cefdinir, commonly sold under the brand name Omnicef, is a cephalosporin antibiotic used to treat a variety of bacterial infections. It is not effective against viral infections such as the common cold or flu. For optimal results, cefdinir should be taken at evenly spaced intervals, and the full prescribed course should be completed, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Certain medications can bind to cefdinir, reducing its absorption. Common side effects of cefdinir include diarrhea, headache, and nausea. It may also cause stools to appear reddish, particularly if taken with iron products. While rare, cefdinir can lead to a severe intestinal condition caused by Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile), which may occur during treatment or weeks to months after therapy has ended. Prolonged or repeated use of cefdinir may result in oral thrush or vaginal yeast infections. Serious allergic reactions to cefdinir are rare but possible. Before starting cefdinir, patients should inform their healthcare provider if they are allergic to cefdinir, penicillins, or other cephalosporin antibiotics, or if they have any other allergies. The medication may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Cefdinir may also reduce the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. During pregnancy, cefdinir should only be used when clearly needed. It is not known to pass into breast milk. Drug interactions may alter the effectiveness of cefdinir or increase the risk of side effects. Patients should maintain a list of all medications and supplements they are taking and share it with their healthcare provider. Cefdinir may interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as some diabetic urine tests, potentially causing false results. In the event of an overdose, individuals experiencing severe symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing should call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). For non-emergency overdoses, U.S. residents can contact the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. Cefdinir should be stored at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and not in the bathroom. Medications should not be flushed down the toilet or poured into drains unless instructed to do so. Expired or unused medication should be properly discarded. Patients should adhere to all medical and laboratory appointments while taking cefdinir, as kidney function tests may be required. If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as remembered. If it is near the time of the next dose, the missed dose should be skipped, and the next dose should be taken at the regular time. Doubling doses should be avoided.
